title: Europe's Worst Heatwave on Record Has Killed Over 1,000 in France. Two Million Indians Live in Its Path.
excerpt: Scientists say the 40°C-plus temperatures shattering records from Germany to Britain would have been 'virtually impossible' without climate change. The same forces are weakening India's monsoon.
body:
More than 1,000 people have died in France alone during what scientists are calling the worst heatwave ever recorded in Europe, and the numbers are expected to climb.

The French public health agency said most of the fatalities involved older people, warning that the final toll would rise as reports came in from residential care homes and private residences. Across the continent, 150 million people are living under extreme heat conditions as temperatures have exceeded 40°C (104°F) in Germany, France, the Czech Republic, and parts of Scandinavia.

"Right now 150 million people are living under extreme heat, hundreds have died, schools are shut, grids are buckling," World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X. "We were warned."

## Records Shattered Across the Continent

The scale is staggering. Germany recorded a new all-time high of 41.5°C in Saxony-Anhalt on Saturday, topping a record set just the day before. Denmark registered 37°C north of Aarhus — the highest since measurements began in 1874. The Czech Republic hit 40.9°C north of Prague. Britain recorded its hottest June day at 36.4°C, and in France, western regions reached 43°C earlier in the week.

Night-time temperatures have been equally brutal. Parts of Spain have not dropped below 30°C after dark, and Bratislava recorded its hottest night on record. The combination of relentless daytime heat and no overnight relief is what kills.

Scientists from the World Weather Attribution group said the heatwave would have been "virtually impossible" without human-caused climate change. A similar June heatwave in 1976 would have been about 3.5°C cooler. Night-time temperatures of this intensity are now 100 times more likely than they would have been just two decades ago.

"This event would not have been possible in June without climate change," said Dr Theodore Keeping, a researcher at Imperial College London. "The three-day night-time temperatures would not have been possible at any time of year without climate change."

## The Human Cost Beyond the Numbers

Infrastructure is buckling under the strain. Power grids in France and Germany are struggling to meet surging demand for air conditioning. Deutsche Bahn told passengers to avoid train travel due to the risk of wildfire-related disruptions and rail buckling. Schools have closed across multiple countries. Cultural landmarks, including some of Paris's most visited museums, have shut their doors.

In Berlin, where temperatures hit 39°C, police deployed water cannons to lightly spray residents trying to cool down — a surreal image in a city where the same vehicles are typically associated with crowd control.

At care homes in London, staff handed out fruit juice and water to dementia patients in shaded gardens. "When they've got dementia, they forget to ask about whether they feel thirsty," said one care home manager.

## The Indian Diaspora in Europe

The heatwave carries particular weight for the more than two million people of Indian origin living across Europe, concentrated in the United Kingdom, Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Italy.

Many diaspora families include elderly relatives who moved to Europe decades ago, when summers rarely required air conditioning and homes were designed to retain heat, not shed it. Indian-origin communities in the UK's Midlands and London, where humidity has reached unprecedented levels, are among those most exposed. Dew-point temperatures in British cities have reached the low 20s — conditions more associated with Mumbai than Manchester.

For the diaspora, the heatwave also reinforces an uncomfortable parallel. India and Pakistan have endured their own sustained deadly heat since April, part of the same climate pattern now pushing heat anomalies into Europe. El Niño, which Australia's weather bureau has declared active, is expected to worsen conditions across South and Southeast Asia in the coming months — threatening India's already-weak monsoon season.

## A Climate Story That Connects Both Homes

The science is unambiguous. Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent. Greenhouse gas emissions have raised global average temperatures by about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels, and the effects are accelerating.

For Indian-origin communities in Europe — many of whom maintain deep connections with family in India — this is not an abstract policy debate. The heatwave in Paris and the failed monsoon in Maharashtra are two faces of the same crisis, driven by the same physics, affecting the same extended families.

"Nature is angry with us because we destroy everything," said 97-year-old Lucine Nazikian, a resident of a London care home, in a moment of clarity that cut through the policy jargon.

The WHO's Tedros put it more formally: "The phenomenon of the 'once-in-a-generation' heatwave is now occurring nearly annually."

Temperatures are expected to ease slightly in Western Europe in the coming days as the heat dome shifts east. But for the families still counting their dead, and for the cities still learning to cope, the respite will be temporary.

*Sources: Reuters, World Health Organization, World Weather Attribution, IFLScience, New Scientist, Phys.org*
